newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian leader urges support as parties eye vote.
newsitem.headline: Algerian leader urges support as parties eye vote.

text.p: Algeria's leadership on Sunday holds a second day of a crucial conference, spurred by calls from President Liamine Zeroual to back reform for multi-party democracy and free Algeria of radical Moslem militancy.

Surrounded by heavy security on the opening day on Saturday, many of the 1,000 politicians praised the conference aim of laying foundations for a democratic system for the country's 29 million people.
Residents of Algiers said there was little public interest in the meeting. "We have heard of talks to resolve the crisis so many times before," said one.
Two of the main secular opposition parties are boycotting the meeting, with one of them accusing Zeroual of trying to impose "institutionalised dictatorship".
The radical Islamists' main party is barred.
In the hall, planned elections next year dominated the speeches of many of those politicians attending.

Boualem Benhamouda, head of the former ruling National Liberation Front (FLN), said: "The authorities are also called to lay down the right conditions to hold legislative and local elections by ensuring equal opportunities for the parties..."
Benhamouda's party is seen as the main one taking part, alongside the legal Hamas movement, whose leader Mafhoud Nahnah won more than 2.9 million votes in last November's presidential election.

Abdallah Djaballah, leader of Ennahda, another legal Islamist party, called on Zeroual to free all detained militants and end the state of emergency imposed in February 1992 which politicians says has effectively frozen party activity.
The emergency was imposed after violence erupted following the authorities' cancellation of a general election in which the now-banned Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a huge lead.
Zeroual, who told the gathering that "abject terrorism has been firmly rejected by the Algerian people", said Algeria "has to face the next election dates to complete its institutional structures".
He was referring to a referendum to change the constitution which he plans within three months and his pledge to hold general and local elections next year.

The government-run newspaper el Djoumhouria said: "The participants at the conference will draw the future lines of the country...pluralism and democracy and elected institutions, while they condemn the means leading to armed opposition".

But outside the conference hall, in the Palais des Nations 20 km (12 miles) from Algiers, a heavy deployment of armed troops, gendarmes and police underscored that Moslem guerrillas still haunt the authorities.
Algerian state-run television showed old footage of troops parading in Algiers streets as well as shots of nationalist guerrillas fighting former French colonial armed forces.
"The platform, which will be submitted to the conference, should be the base on which democratic Algeria will be built...," said Nourredine Boukrouh, leader of the Algerian Renewal Party (PRA).
The authorities blame radical Islamists for the deaths of some 50,000 people since January 1992 when the Algerian leadership cancelled the general election.
Algeria's "National Conference of Understanding" follows nearly two years of tortuous talks, and a largely-boycotted similar conference in January 1994.
